title: Paul Bongiorno on how Labor are taking the recent spate of polls showing a surgi...
text:

Midweek, as missiles and drones shattered a so-called ceasefire in the Middle East, Anthony Albanese unveiled his strategy to intercept the Exocet that Pauline Hanson has aimed at his government.

Newspoll set the scene for the week, recording for the first time that One Nation was heading Labor in the primary vote. It was only by one point – 31-30 – which is statistically lineball but significant when taken with other polls this week that were recording even bigger leads for the insurgent disrupter.

Although the prime minister was given an opportunity at every news conference he held after the Newspoll release to attack Hanson or her burgeoning cohort of supporters, he steadfastly resisted.

He was asked how he explained the rise of One Nation and who he would prefer to face at the election – Angus Taylor or Pauline Hanson.

“Well, those are matters for the Australian people, effectively,” Albanese replied, adding that he respects the Australian people “and the judgements that they make”.

There was no Hillary Clinton-like dismissal of Hanson’s supporters as a “basket of deplorables”. Albanese is too astute a politician to fall into that trap. Indeed, an analysis of the polls shows One Nation is not just appealing to deplorables – it is becoming mainstream in large swathes of regional and rural Australia and even knocking on the doors of the cities.

Rather than scoff, the Labor leader accepted the evidence of the published and private polls to identify with the millions of Australians flagging an interest in voting for One Nation.

“Many people feel that the system isn’t working for them,” he said, adding that they believe “they’re working for the economy, not the economy working for them, that they are working hard, struggling to save, can’t get their own roof over their head”.

The challenge Albanese has to confront is not only to leverage all the powers of incumbency to his cause but to convince people he is delivering for them now.

According to a Labor source, the party’s research is picking up a ‘hesitancy’ among voters when confronted with the prospect of Pauline Hanson being prime minister. The observation is: ‘They are not sure they want her to run the country.’

This is how he framed Australia’s response to renewed hostilities in the Persian Gulf further destabilising the global economy and energy supplies, particularly to our part of the world.

Albanese repeated Australia’s calls for de-escalation – something Donald Trump has claimed is close 38 times, according to United States media reports. Rather than dwell on this uncertainty, Albanese pointed to Labor’s delivery of emergency supplies of fuel in the face of media and opposition claims the country would run out by Easter and restrictions would have to be imposed.

He said there was a problem leading to dangerous hoarding that was easy to “identify” and “amplify”, but what his government did was “provide solutions” and there is now more fuel in Australia than there was on February 28, when the conflict with Iran started.

There are no complaints from One Nation or the Coalition about the millions of dollars this spot buying on the world market is costing, nor any recognition that it took a concerted personal commitment on the prime minister’s part to shuttle diplomacy around the region.

Labor, Albanese claims, is now “the only party in the mainstream of Australian politics that is engaged with serious solutions”.

This is the core message Labor will continue to hammer home. Strategists believe this will render less potent One Nation’s latest slogan as it seeks donations: “Fire the liar!”

The Liberals, too, are counting on Labor’s broken promises on taxation reform to undermine trust in Albanese.

The “lie” is very much in the eye of the beholder. Albanese certainly ruled out “50 times” on his own reckoning any such changes during the election campaign. He now says his position has changed because political and economic circumstances have changed.

Certainly, the millions of dollars Labor was directing on the supply side were not delivering the desired results, as the housing market continued to be distorted by tax concessions subsidising investors at the expense of first-home buyers.

The policy is already showing signs at weekend auctions of helping to address the housing crisis for first-home buyers, even before it has been legislated.

On that front, the manager of Greens business in the Senate, Sarah Hanson-Young, told Radio National Breakfast her party had been campaigning for a long time for changes to the capital gains tax discount and negative gearing and they would use next week’s inquiry to look for “improvements” rather than to vote against the changes.

Hanson-Young is foreshadowing a tougher time for the National Disability Insurance Scheme reforms, which the Greens do not support and will do “nothing to facilitate that bill’s passage over the next two weeks”.

It looks as though the Coalition, which will support the changes, will get its wish to frustrate the government’s timetable with a longer inquiry.

One seasoned Labor strategist says the “dinkum” policy contest at the election is two budgets away and Labor needs to focus on governing.

This is a reality check on hysteria that seems to presume the arguments and factors consuming the political debate now will be exactly the same in May 2028.

The opinion polls at this stage are more like market research, giving insight into what is happening but with plenty of time for the players to adjust their games.

It is useful to recall that the first nine polls in the 2025 election year had the Coalition leading two-party preferred.

Labor had been trailing in the poll average since October 2024 and only pulled ahead once the election was announced on March 28.

The average of the final polls had Labor on 52.6 per cent, whereas the actual result was 55.2 per cent, producing a massive historic landslide.

Assistant minister to the prime minister Patrick Gorman says it’s not uncommon for voters to look at different political options midterm. He told ABC TV he was “as relaxed and unbothered by the polls at this point in the political cycle” as he was at previous points in the political cycle.

One of Angus Taylor’s closest supporters in the parliamentary Liberal Party, Garth Hamilton, believes the Australian people want to see change both in the direction of the country and in the direction of the various political parties.

Hamilton concedes One Nation is a “very strong populist movement”, but he says it is not yet at the levels of Nick Xenophon’s SA-BEST party, which contested the 2018 South Australian election.

He said Xenophon’s party “got up to 35 per cent … but failed to win any seats in the lower house”.

According to a Labor source, the party’s research is picking up a “hesitancy” among voters when confronted with the prospect of Pauline Hanson being prime minister. The observation is: “They are not sure they want her to run the country.”

This was the issue that finally stymied Xenophon’s push, according to observers in Adelaide, and he by any measure was a much more middle-of-the-road voice than Hanson.

Labor’s Shayne Neumann, who holds the outer Ipswich seat of Blair that Hanson unsuccessfully contested in 1998, is confident voters will see through her party. He told The Saturday Paper One Nation “is not a serious party” and that they offer “simplistic nonsense” in line with economic illiteracy.

Still, Hanson has garnered more attention than she has for much of her controversial 30 years in politics, and has become something of a darling of the News Corp tabloids.

The Sunday Herald Sun claims she is as popular with crowds as Bob Hawke was in the 1980s. Columnist James Campbell wrote that the last time he saw the sort of political enthusiasm currently on display for Pauline Hanson was 10 years ago “at the Republican convention in Cleveland that nominated Donald Trump”.

This is dangerously close to confusing “celebrity” with credibility and voting intention. Shayne Neumann recalled two Labor prime ministers in his memory – Gough Whitlam and Paul Keating – who drew huge, enthusiastic crowds only to be smashed at their last elections.

According to the Labor strategist, Hanson has been in the top five media stories for most of the past two months. She “gives a channel for real-world frustrations, and that drives opinion polls”.

Angus Taylor, who has seen support for the Liberal Party go backwards since he replaced Sussan Ley as leader, is blaming Albanese for his party’s parlous state.

Taylor is quoted in The Sydney Morning Herald as saying Albanese’s broken promises have eroded trust in the political system. He says we are “paying part of the price for it”, but he is counting for some space “over the winter break to talk more about our positive plan”.

That plan is already facing unflattering scrutiny. The Australia Institute analysed what tax indexation would have delivered since 1996 compared with what Labor and Liberal governments have delivered by way of tax relief over those years.

Far from taxing by “stealth”, as Taylor claims, scales left to automatic indexation would have seen average taxpayers $7583 a year worse off compared with the present tax scales.

There’s time for everyone to take stock.

Paul Bongiorno is a columnist for The Saturday Paper and a 35-year veteran of the Canberra Press Gallery.
